title: My dream trip

opts: Я не хочу ехать потому что...

writingModel: My dream destination is Istanbul — the largest city in Turkey and one of the most extraordinary cities in the world. It is located at the meeting point of two continents, Europe and Asia, on both sides of the Bosphorus Strait. I have wanted to visit Istanbul since I was twelve years old, when I first saw a photograph of the Blue Mosque reflected in the water at sunset. Since that moment, I have read books about it, watched documentaries about it, and saved hundreds of photographs of its skyline. Istanbul is not just my dream trip — it is the journey I am working towards, step by step, every single day.

The place I most want to see is the Hagia Sophia — an ancient building that stands in the heart of the old city, next to the famous Blue Mosque. Between these two enormous structures, there is an open courtyard facing the sky. In front of the Hagia Sophia, there is a wide square called Sultanahmet Square, and around it are gardens, fountains, and ancient stone walls. I would spend my first morning there, sitting on the steps of a fountain opposite the great dome, looking up at the building above me and trying to understand how people built something so magnificent over fifteen hundred years ago.

On my second day, I would walk through the Grand Bazaar — one of the oldest covered markets in the world. It is in the heart of the European side of the city, not far from the waterfront. Inside, thousands of small shops stand one next to the other in long covered streets that run across the market from entrance to entrance. I would walk along the narrow alleys, past shops selling spices, lamps, carpets, and jewellery. After the bazaar, I would take a ferry across the Bosphorus — from the European side of Istanbul to the Asian side — and stand in two continents within the space of twenty minutes.

In the evenings, I would sit in a small café opposite the water, drink strong Turkish tea from a small glass, and write in my notebook. Istanbul is a city for dreamers — it is ancient and modern at the same time, noisy and peaceful at the same time. I would stay there for five days. On my last evening, I would walk along the waterfront at sunset and look back at the city skyline — the minarets rising above the rooftops, the lights reflecting in the water far below.

For me, this trip would be unforgettable because Istanbul connects history, architecture, and culture in one extraordinary place. It would teach me things no textbook ever could — about ancient civilisations, about people, about beauty. And when I came back to WKU and sat down at my desk in Uralsk, I would have stories to tell for the rest of my life. Visiting Istanbul is not just a dream. It is a plan. And one day — I will go.
